description: What does VLOOKUP do?
explanation: VLOOKUP searches for a value in the first column of a range and returns a value from another column of the matching row.
choice0: Sorts a table by its first column
choice1: Finds a value in the first column and returns a value from the same row
choice2: Counts how many times a value appears
choice3: Checks whether two columns are identical

description: In =VLOOKUP(A2, D:F, 3, FALSE), what does the 3 mean?
explanation: The third argument is the column index within the lookup range, so 3 means the third column, F.
choice0: Return the value from the third column of the range
choice1: Search only the first three rows
choice2: Allow three characters of difference when matching
choice3: Round the result to three decimal places

description: Why is FALSE the safer final argument for VLOOKUP?
explanation: FALSE demands an exact match. TRUE allows an approximate match and quietly returns wrong rows on unsorted data.
choice0: It makes the formula run faster
choice1: It allows the lookup column to contain text
choice2: It requires an exact match instead of an approximate one
choice3: It hides errors when no match is found

description: What is a well-known limitation of VLOOKUP?
explanation: VLOOKUP can only look to the right, because the search column must be the first column of the range.
choice0: It cannot handle more than 100 rows
choice1: It only works on numbers
choice2: It cannot be copied down a column
choice3: It cannot return a value from a column to the left of the search column

description: What advantage does XLOOKUP have over VLOOKUP?
explanation: XLOOKUP takes the search and result ranges separately, so it can look in either direction and does not break when columns move.
choice0: It can return values from columns on either side of the search column
choice1: It does not need a search value
choice2: It can only be used once per sheet
choice3: It automatically sorts the data first

description: What does the INDEX and MATCH combination achieve?
explanation: MATCH finds the position of a value and INDEX returns whatever sits at that position, giving a flexible two-way lookup.
choice0: It merges two tables into one
choice1: MATCH finds the row position and INDEX returns the value there
choice2: It counts matching values across two ranges
choice3: It sorts one column to match another

description: What does =IFERROR(A1/B1, 0) do?
explanation: IFERROR returns the first argument normally, but substitutes the second whenever the first produces an error.
choice0: Always returns 0
choice1: Returns an error message when the division fails
choice2: Returns the division result, or 0 if it produces an error
choice3: Checks whether A1 and B1 are both numbers

description: What does =COUNTIFS() add over =COUNTIF()?
explanation: COUNTIFS applies several conditions at once and counts only the rows that satisfy all of them.
choice0: It tests several conditions at once
choice1: It counts text as well as numbers
choice2: It counts across several sheets
choice3: It ignores hidden rows

description: What does =SUMIFS(C:C, A:A, "north", B:B, ">100") total?
explanation: SUMIFS adds values from the sum range only for rows meeting every condition, here region north and value over 100.
choice0: Every value in column C
choice1: The values in C where either condition holds
choice2: The count of rows meeting both conditions
choice3: The values in C where the region is north and column B exceeds 100

description: What does =AVERAGEIF(A:A, ">0") calculate?
explanation: It averages only the values that satisfy the condition, ignoring the rest.
choice0: The average of every value in column A
choice1: The average of the values greater than zero
choice2: The count of values greater than zero
choice3: The sum of values greater than zero

description: What does =AND(A1>0, B1>0) return?
explanation: AND returns TRUE only when every condition it is given is true.
choice0: TRUE only when both conditions hold
choice1: TRUE when at least one condition holds
choice2: The sum of A1 and B1
choice3: The larger of A1 and B1

description: What does =OR(A1="yes", B1="yes") return?
explanation: OR returns TRUE when at least one of its conditions is true.
choice0: TRUE only when both cells say yes
choice1: The text yes
choice2: TRUE when at least one cell says yes
choice3: The number of cells saying yes

description: What does nesting IF functions let you do?
explanation: Placing an IF inside another IF lets a formula choose between more than two outcomes.
choice0: Repeat a calculation many times
choice1: Choose between more than two possible results
choice2: Apply a condition to a whole column at once
choice3: Hide rows that fail the condition

description: What does =NOT(A1>10) return when A1 holds 15?
explanation: A1>10 is TRUE, and NOT reverses it, so the result is FALSE.
choice0: TRUE
choice2: An error
choice3: FALSE

description: What does =LEFT("invoice", 3) return?
explanation: LEFT takes the given number of characters from the start of the text.
choice0: "inv"
choice1: "ice"
choice2: "invoice"

description: What does =RIGHT("2024-06", 2) return?
explanation: RIGHT takes characters from the end of the text, here the last two.

description: What does =MID("abcdef", 2, 3) return?
explanation: MID starts at the given position and takes the given number of characters, so it starts at b and takes three.
choice0: "abc"
choice1: "cde"
choice2: "bcd"
choice3: "def"

description: What does =TRIM() do to a piece of text?
explanation: TRIM strips leading and trailing spaces and collapses repeated inner spaces to one.
choice0: Removes leading, trailing and repeated inner spaces
choice1: Shortens the text to a fixed length
choice2: Removes all spaces including those between words
choice3: Removes punctuation

description: Why is TRIM useful before comparing two columns of names?
explanation: Invisible trailing spaces make otherwise identical text compare as different, and TRIM removes them.
choice0: It converts the names to the same case
choice1: It sorts the names alphabetically
choice2: It removes duplicate names
choice3: It removes stray spaces that would make identical names look different

description: What does the & operator do in ="Mr " & A1?
explanation: The ampersand joins text, so this puts the title in front of whatever A1 holds.
choice0: Adds A1 to the number of characters in "Mr "
choice1: Joins the text with the contents of A1
choice2: Formats A1 as a name
choice3: Compares "Mr " with A1

description: When copying =B\$2 down a column, what changes?
explanation: The dollar sign locks the row, so the row stays 2 while only the column could shift, which it does not when copying downwards.
choice0: Both the column and the row shift
choice1: Only the row shifts
choice2: Nothing, because the locked row 2 keeps the reference on B2
choice3: The formula turns into an error

description: When would you use a mixed reference such as \$B2?
explanation: Locking only the column lets a formula fill across and down while always reading from column B.
choice0: When the formula must always read column B but follow the row it is in
choice1: When the value should never change
choice2: When referring to another workbook
choice3: When the reference points at a chart

description: What is a named range?
explanation: A named range gives a meaningful label to a cell or range so formulas can refer to it by name.
choice0: A range that has been sorted
choice1: A label given to a cell or range so formulas can use the name
choice2: A range copied to a second sheet
choice3: A range protected against editing

description: What does Remove Duplicates do to a selected range?
explanation: It deletes rows whose selected columns repeat an earlier row, keeping the first occurrence.
choice0: Highlights the duplicate rows
choice1: Moves duplicates to a new sheet
choice2: Counts how many duplicates exist
choice3: Deletes repeated rows, keeping the first of each

description: What does Text to Columns do?
explanation: It splits one column into several by breaking each value at a chosen delimiter such as a comma.
choice0: Splits one column into several at a chosen separator
choice1: Converts numbers into text
choice2: Joins several columns into one
choice3: Renames the column headers

description: What does data validation on a cell do?
explanation: It restricts what may be entered, for example to a list of allowed values or a numeric range.
choice0: Checks formulas for errors
choice1: Highlights cells that differ from their neighbours
choice2: Restricts what values may be entered
choice3: Locks the cell permanently

description: Why is a drop-down list built with data validation useful for a data-entry column?
explanation: It restricts entries to an agreed set of values, which prevents typos and inconsistent spellings.
choice0: It makes the column sort faster
choice1: It prevents typos and inconsistent spellings
choice2: It compresses the file
choice3: It hides the column from other users

description: Which chart type is best for comparing a value across a handful of categories?
explanation: A bar or column chart makes category comparisons easy to read.
choice0: A bar or column chart
choice1: A pie chart
choice2: A scatter plot
choice3: A line chart

description: Which chart type is best for showing how a value changes over time?
explanation: A line chart shows a trend across an ordered time axis clearly.
choice0: A pie chart
choice1: A stacked bar chart
choice2: A line chart
choice3: A doughnut chart

description: Why are pie charts often a poor choice?
explanation: People judge angles and areas badly, so differences between similar slices are hard to read, especially with many categories.
choice0: They cannot show percentages
choice1: Similar slice sizes are hard to compare accurately
choice2: They cannot be printed in colour
choice3: They only work with two categories

description: Why can starting a bar chart axis above zero be misleading?
explanation: Truncating the axis exaggerates the differences between bars, because bar length no longer matches the value.
choice0: It makes the chart harder to print
choice1: It hides the axis labels
choice2: It reverses the order of the bars
choice3: It exaggerates the differences between bars

description: What does =ROUNDUP(4.1, 0) return?
explanation: ROUNDUP always rounds away from zero, so 4.1 becomes 5 even though it is nearer 4.

description: What does =ABS(-12) return?
explanation: ABS returns the magnitude of a number without its sign.
choice3: An error

description: What does =MEDIAN() return that =AVERAGE() does not?
explanation: The median is the middle value once sorted, so unlike the mean it is barely affected by extreme outliers.
choice0: The most common value
choice1: The range of the values
choice2: The middle value, which resists outliers
choice3: The total divided by the count

description: What does =RANK() tell you about a value?
explanation: RANK reports the position of a value within a list, such as third largest.
choice0: Its position within a list of values
choice1: How many times it appears
choice2: Its percentage of the total
choice3: Whether it is above average

description: What is stored behind the scenes when a cell shows a date?
explanation: Dates are stored as serial numbers counting days from a fixed origin, which is why they can be added and subtracted.
choice0: The date as plain text
choice1: A special date object that cannot be used in arithmetic
choice2: The day, month and year in three hidden cells
choice3: A number counting days from a fixed starting date

description: What does subtracting one date cell from another give you?
explanation: Because dates are serial numbers, the difference is a count of days.
choice0: An error
choice1: The number of days between them
choice2: The later of the two dates
choice3: The number of months between them

description: What does #N/A mean as the result of a lookup?
explanation: The lookup ran correctly but found no matching value.
choice0: No matching value was found
choice1: The formula divided by zero
choice2: The function name is unknown
choice3: The referenced sheet was deleted

description: What does the #VALUE! error usually indicate?
explanation: A formula was given the wrong kind of input, such as text where a number was expected.
choice0: A deleted cell reference
choice1: A division by zero
choice2: The wrong type of input, such as text where a number is needed
choice3: A circular reference

description: What is a circular reference?
explanation: A formula that depends, directly or through a chain, on its own cell, so it can never settle on a value.
choice0: Two sheets that reference each other
choice1: A formula that depends on its own cell
choice2: A reference to a cell in a closed workbook
choice3: A range that wraps around the edge of the sheet

description: What does =CONCAT() or the & operator do to numbers?
explanation: Joining turns the numbers into text, so the result is characters placed side by side rather than a sum.
choice0: Places them side by side as text
choice1: Adds them together
choice2: Multiplies them
choice3: Returns an error

description: Why can two visually identical cells fail an equality test?
explanation: One may hold a number and the other the same digits stored as text, or one may carry an invisible trailing space.
choice0: Because equality tests are unreliable
choice1: Because one cell is formatted in bold
choice2: Because the cells are on different rows
choice3: Because one may be text while the other is a number, or hold hidden spaces

description: What does =VALUE("42") return?
explanation: VALUE converts text that looks like a number into an actual number that arithmetic can use.
choice0: The text "42"
choice1: The number 42
choice2: An error
choice3: TRUE

description: What does Paste Special with Values only achieve?
explanation: It pastes the results of the copied formulas rather than the formulas themselves, freezing the numbers in place.
choice0: Pastes the results without the underlying formulas
choice1: Pastes the formatting only
choice2: Pastes the formulas without their results
choice3: Pastes a link back to the original cells

description: Why would you paste with Transpose?
explanation: Transpose swaps rows and columns, turning a horizontal layout into a vertical one or the reverse.
choice0: To remove formatting during the paste
choice1: To paste only visible cells
choice2: To swap rows and columns
choice3: To paste into every selected sheet at once

description: What does a custom number format change?
explanation: It changes only how the value is displayed. The underlying value stays exactly as stored.
choice0: The stored value and its display
choice1: Only how the value is displayed
choice2: The formula that produced the value
choice3: The data type of the cell permanently

description: What does =COUNTBLANK(A1:A20) return?
explanation: COUNTBLANK reports how many cells in the range are empty.
choice0: How many cells contain numbers
choice1: How many cells contain text
choice2: How many cells contain formulas
choice3: How many cells are empty

description: Why does a lookup fail when the key is a number in one table and text in another?
explanation: A lookup matches value and type, so the number 100 and the text "100" are not considered equal.
choice0: A number and the same digits stored as text are not equal
choice1: Lookups can only match text
choice2: Lookups always ignore the first row
choice3: Numbers are rounded before matching

description: What does sorting a table by two levels, such as region then sales, achieve?
explanation: The first key orders the rows into groups and the second orders the rows within each group.
choice0: It sorts by whichever column has more values
choice1: It sorts the columns rather than the rows
choice2: It groups by region and orders sales within each region
choice3: It applies two filters at once

description: What does =IF(ISBLANK(A1), "missing", A1) return when A1 is empty?
explanation: ISBLANK is TRUE for an empty cell, so IF returns its second argument, the text missing.
choice0: The contents of A1
choice1: "missing"
choice2: An error
choice3: FALSE
